how-required-status-checks-go-stale.html.text:
← Required Checks Drift Check

How a required status check goes stale, and how to fix it

Branch protection's "Require status checks to pass" list is a list of names. GitHub never re-derives it from your workflow files — it just waits for something to report a status under each name. Three ordinary changes leave a name nothing will ever satisfy again:

1. The job was renamed

jobs:
  build:            # was required as "build"
    name: Build and Test   # now reports as "Build and Test" instead

Adding a name: to a job that previously had none — or changing an existing one — changes the check-run name GitHub reports. Branch protection still has the old name. Every new pull request now waits on a status that will never arrive.

2. The job was removed or its id changed

Deleting a job outright, or renaming its job id when it has no name: override, is the same failure by a different route: the name branch protection requires simply stops being produced.

3. The workflow dropped its pull_request trigger

on:
  push:            # used to also list pull_request
    branches: [main]

GitHub can only post a status onto a pull request from a run that pull request triggered. A workflow that only runs on: push can have a job with exactly the right name and still never satisfy a required check on a PR — this looks identical to a rename from the branch-protection screen, but the fix is different: restore the trigger, don't rename anything.

Fixing it

Either remove the stale name from Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules, or make a current job report under that exact name again (an explicit name: override is the least disruptive way, since it doesn't require touching the job id or its steps).

Paste your required checks and workflow YAML into Required Checks Drift Check to find every stale or no-pull-request-trigger name across every workflow file at once, or run the CLI in your own repository:

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection > protection.json
python3 check.py --required-checks protection.json --fail-on-stale

That exits with a nonzero status if any required check is stale — wire it into your own CI, or run it once after any branch-protection or workflow change.

REQUIRED CHECKS DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is a required status check stuck forever?

Branch protection matches a required status check by exact name. Rename a job, delete it, or drop its workflow's pull_request trigger, and nothing warns you — GitHub just never reports that name again, and every future pull request sits at “Expected — Waiting for status to be reported” until someone notices. Paste your required check names and workflow YAML below to find every one that is already stuck.

Nothing is uploaded. What you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own — not even to read your branch protection settings for you.

1. Paste your required status check names

From Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules → Require status checks to pass, one per line — or paste the JSON from gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection directly, contexts array and all. Leave this blank to just see the check names your workflows would currently report.

2. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ that could produce one of the checks above.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

Required check nameStatusWhat this means

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                                        # list computed check names for .github/workflows
python3 check.py --required-checks names.txt            # compare against a plain-text list
python3 check.py --required-checks protection.json      # or the branch-protection API's own JSON
python3 check.py --required-checks names.txt --format json
python3 check.py --required-checks names.txt --fail-on-stale   # exit 2 if any required check is stale

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Fetch your own required-checks JSON with gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection > protection.json and feed it straight in.

Common questions

Why does a pull request get stuck at “Expected — Waiting for status to be reported”?

Branch protection matches required status checks by exact name. If the job that used to report that name was renamed, removed, or its workflow no longer triggers on pull_request, GitHub has nothing left to satisfy that name — every future pull request sits pending forever, with nothing in the pull request itself explaining why.

Does this tool read my branch protection settings for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. Paste the required check names (from Settings → Branches, or the JSON from the GitHub API) and your workflow YAML, and the comparison happens entirely in this page.

How does it compute a job's check name?

A job's name: field if it has one, otherwise its job id, exactly as GitHub Actions reports it. A matrix job gets " (value1, value2, ...)" appended for each combination, in the matrix's declared order.

What can't it verify?

A dynamic matrix built from an expression like fromJson(...), or one using include/exclude, cannot be enumerated statically — those jobs are reported as unverifiable rather than guessed at. A job that calls a reusable workflow (uses: a .yml file) uses a different naming convention this tool does not compute, for the same reason.

Does a clean result mean my branch protection is fully correct?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented thing: whether each required check name matches a job that would report on a pull request today. It is not a full audit of your branch protection rules or CI configuration.

A stale required check is one specific way branch protection can silently stop working. vs-reading-every-workflow-file-by-hand.h.text:
← Required Checks Drift Check

This checker vs. reading every workflow file by hand

GitHub's own UI gives you nothing to go on: a pull request stuck at "Expected — Waiting for status to be reported" names no cause. Tracing it by hand means opening every workflow file and re-deriving each job's current check name yourself — and doing it again the next time you suspect drift.

What reading the workflows by hand gets you

For one workflow with one job, this is genuinely faster than pasting anything into a page: open the file, read the job's name: or its id, compare it to what Settings → Branches requires, done. It stops scaling the moment a repository has more than a couple of workflows, any matrix jobs, or a required-check list nobody has re-audited since it was set up — which is precisely when drift is most likely to have already happened.

What this checker does instead

Paste your required check names (from Settings → Branches, or the branch-protection API's JSON) and one or more workflow files, and it computes every job's current reported name — its name: field if set, otherwise its job id, with matrix combinations expanded in declared order — and flags every required name nothing can currently satisfy. A dynamic matrix or a reusable-workflow call is reported unverifiable rather than guessed at, so a result never claims more certainty than the YAML actually gives it.

Reading every workflow file by handThis checker
Works for one workflow, one job. Scales badly across a dozen workflows and several matrix jobs, and has to be redone from scratch after every workflow edit. Computes every job's current check name from the pasted YAML in one pass, matrix combinations included, every time you run it.
A quick read checks the job's name: line and stops there — which passes a workflow that dropped its pull_request trigger, because the name is still correct even though the job can never report on a pull request again. Checks the trigger as well as the name, so a required check pointed at a push-only workflow is flagged the same as a renamed or removed job.
Guesses at a matrix job's reported name by eye, which is exactly the case most likely to be gotten wrong by hand (the appended combination text has to match GitHub's own ordering exactly). Expands a static matrix in its declared order and reports a dynamic one as unverifiable rather than a guess either way could be wrong about.
Gives you no artifact to hand to a teammate or re-run after the next workflow change — the check lived in your head for as long as you were looking at the files. Wires into CI with check.py --fail-on-stale, so a newly-drifted required check is caught the moment it happens rather than the next time someone happens to notice a stuck PR.

Common questions

Why can't I just read the workflow files myself?

You can, and for one workflow with one job it is faster than pasting anything anywhere. The problem is scale and drift: a repository with a dozen workflows and matrix jobs across several of them means re-deriving each job's current reported name (its name: field if set, otherwise its job id, with matrix combinations appended) from YAML, by eye, for every job, every time you suspect drift — and doing it again after every workflow edit, because nothing tells you when a rename happened.

What does GitHub's own UI tell me when this happens?

Nothing useful. The pull request sits at "Expected — Waiting for status to be reported" indefinitely, with no message naming which required check is the problem or why. Settings → Branches shows you the required name you configured, but does not check it against what your workflows currently produce — that comparison is exactly what GitHub never runs for you.

Is reading the workflow by hand ever wrong, not just slow?

Yes, in the case that matters most: a workflow that dropped its pull_request trigger. The job can have the exact right name and pass every time it runs, and still never satisfy the required check on a pull request, because it only runs on push. Reading the job's name tells you nothing about its trigger, so a hand check that only looks at name: lines can pass a workflow that is actually broken for this purpose.

Does this tool check my branch protection settings for me?

No. It makes no network calls of any kind and never reads your repository or its settings. You paste the required check names and the workflow YAML yourself, and the comparison runs entirely in this page.

Nothing here says reading a workflow file is a bad habit — it is exactly the right tool for a quick, one-job check. This page describes the point where that habit stops scaling to a real branch-protection list.
